Every number cites — beta ~1.09, R-squared ~0.74, Shapiro-Wilk p-value, VW Group CAAR t-statistic, near-zero CAAR — one live deterministic layer already produced; LLM supplies surrounding prose, runtime guard drop recommendation citing diagnostic match.
code: # Requires an LLM provider and, for Anthropic/OpenAI-compatible providers, # the optional `httr2` + `jsonlite` Suggests and an API key in the environment. p      <- provider("anthropic")                 # or provider("openai_compatible", ...) advice <- es_advise(diag, task_type = "recommend_stat", provider = p) print(advice) Event Study Advice ================== Source:         anthropic Task type:      recommend_stat Deterministic:  FALSE Recommendations: 1  Interpretation:   The market model is well specified across all four events (median estimation-window   R-squared approximately 0.74), so the estimated normal-return benchmark is credible.   Against that benchmark the Dieselgate disclosure produced sharply asymmetric effects   across the two groups. For the VW Group (VOW.DE and PAH3.DE), the average abnormal   return was approximately -17% on day +1 and -13% on day +2, cumulating to a   cumulative average abnormal return (CAAR) of about -39% at day +10 (CAAR   t-statistic approximately -12.6) — a crash that is large, rapid, and   statistically unambiguous. For the peer automakers (BMW.DE, MBG.DE), the CAAR   at day +10 is approximately +1% (t-statistic approximately 0.34), statistically   indistinguishable from zero. The shock is idiosyncratic: there is no measurable   contagion to the broader German automotive sector.    However, the estimation-window residuals fail the Shapiro-Wilk normality test   (p approximately 0.004), which undermines the distributional assumptions of   the standard parametric AR/CAR t-tests, and the two-firm-per-group design means   the cross-sectional t-test's large-sample normal approximation is unreliable.  [1] Consider non-parametric test statistics (Sign Test, Rank Test)     Kind:   stat_choice     Effect: Preserves test size when estimation-window residuals are non-normal.     Evidence:       estimation_window.shapiro_p = 0.0039 (threshold 0.05, below)  Caveats:  - With only two events per group, the cross-sectional t-test's large-sample    approximation is unreliable; lean on the individual event-level time-series    standard errors and non-parametric tests.  - The VW Group crash coincides with heavy news flow and possible confounding    events (regulatory statements, credit-rating actions); attribute the full CAAR    to the Dieselgate disclosure only with that caveat in mind.  - The near-zero Other CAAR supports an idiosyncratic interpretation, but with    two firms per group the power to detect modest contagion is limited.  Advisor Pro (waitlist): richer, corpus-grounded interpretation.

title: Creating Custom Models
text: EventStudy package uses object-oriented model system based R6 classes. Every model inherits ModelBase, defines interface pipeline expects. vignette shows create custom model plug event study workflow.

title: Creating Custom Models
text: models must implement two methods: fit(data_tbl) – Estimate model parameters estimation window. abnormal_returns(data_tbl) – Compute abnormal returns observations (estimation + event windows). fit() method also populate private$.statistics least sigma degree_of_freedom, used test statistics.

title: Creating Custom Models
text: Suppose want industry-adjusted model expected return equals industry index return rather broad market index.
code: library(EventStudy)  IndustryAdjustedModel <- R6::R6Class("IndustryAdjustedModel",   inherit = ModelBase,   public = list(     model_name = "IndustryAdjustedModel",      fit = function(data_tbl) {       # No estimation needed -- just compute statistics       private$.is_fitted <- TRUE       private$calculate_statistics(data_tbl)     },      abnormal_returns = function(data_tbl) {       # AR = firm return - industry index return       # Assumes data_tbl has an 'industry_return' column       data_tbl %>%         dplyr::mutate(abnormal_returns = firm_returns - industry_return)     }   ),   private = list(     calculate_statistics = function(data_tbl) {       estimation_tbl <- data_tbl %>%         dplyr::filter(estimation_window == 1)        residuals <- estimation_tbl$firm_returns - estimation_tbl$industry_return       private$add_residuals(residuals)       private$first_order_autocorrelation(residuals)        sigma <- sd(residuals, na.rm = TRUE)       private$.statistics$sigma <- sigma       private$.statistics$degree_of_freedom <- length(residuals) - 1        # Forecast error correction       event_window_tbl <- data_tbl %>% dplyr::filter(event_window == 1)       private$calculate_forecast_error_correction(         sigma, nrow(estimation_tbl),         estimation_tbl$index_returns,         event_window_tbl$index_returns       )     }   ) )

title: Creating Custom Models
text: model simply computes excess returns risk-free rate:
code: ExcessReturnModel <- R6::R6Class("ExcessReturnModel",   inherit = ModelBase,   public = list(     model_name = "ExcessReturnModel",     risk_free_rate = 0.0001,  # daily risk-free rate      initialize = function(risk_free_rate = 0.0001) {       self$risk_free_rate <- risk_free_rate     },      fit = function(data_tbl) {       private$.is_fitted <- TRUE       estimation_tbl <- data_tbl %>%         dplyr::filter(estimation_window == 1)       residuals <- estimation_tbl$firm_returns - self$risk_free_rate       private$.statistics$sigma <- sd(residuals, na.rm = TRUE)       private$.statistics$degree_of_freedom <- length(residuals) - 1       private$add_residuals(residuals)       private$first_order_autocorrelation(residuals)     },      abnormal_returns = function(data_tbl) {       data_tbl %>%         dplyr::mutate(abnormal_returns = firm_returns - self$risk_free_rate)     }   ) )

title: Creating Custom Test Statistics
text: EventStudy package supports two types test statistics: Single-event statistics – Computed event individually (e.g., AR t-test, CAR t-test) Multi-event statistics – Computed across events group (e.g., Cross-Sectional t-test, Patell Z, Sign test) types inherit TestStatisticBase implement compute() method. vignette walks creating custom test statistics type.

title: Creating Custom Test Statistics
text: Every test statistic must: Inherit TestStatisticBase Set name field (short code used column name results) Implement compute(data_tbl, model) returning tibble single-event tests, data_tbl contains one event’s data model fitted model event. multi-event tests, data_tbl contains events group model nested tibble models.

title: Creating Custom Test Statistics
text: non-parametric test whether abnormal returns event window symmetrically distributed around zero:
code: library(EventStudy)  WilcoxonARTest <- R6::R6Class("WilcoxonARTest",   inherit = TestStatisticBase,   public = list(     name = "WilcoxonAR",      compute = function(data_tbl, model) {       event_data <- data_tbl %>%         dplyr::filter(event_window == 1)        ar <- event_data$abnormal_returns        # Wilcoxon signed-rank test against 0       test_result <- wilcox.test(ar, mu = 0, conf.int = TRUE)        tibble::tibble(         n_obs        = length(ar),         V_statistic  = test_result$statistic,         p_value      = test_result$p.value,         median_ar    = median(ar, na.rm = TRUE),         conf_low     = test_result$conf.int[1],         conf_high    = test_result$conf.int[2]       )     }   ) )

title: Creating Custom Test Statistics
text: non-parametric test comparing distribution AARs normal distribution:
code: KSTest <- R6::R6Class("KSTest",   inherit = TestStatisticBase,   public = list(     name = "KS",      compute = function(data_tbl, model) {       aar_stats <- data_tbl %>%         dplyr::filter(event_window == 1) %>%         dplyr::group_by(relative_index) %>%         dplyr::summarise(           aar        = mean(abnormal_returns, na.rm = TRUE),           n_events   = dplyr::n(),           n_pos      = sum(abnormal_returns > 0, na.rm = TRUE),           n_neg      = sum(abnormal_returns <= 0, na.rm = TRUE),           .groups    = "drop"         ) %>%         dplyr::mutate(caar = cumsum(aar))        # KS test of AARs against normal       ks <- ks.test(aar_stats$aar, "pnorm",                     mean = 0, sd = sd(aar_stats$aar))        aar_stats %>%         dplyr::mutate(           ks_D      = ks$statistic,           ks_pvalue = ks$p.value         )     }   ) )

title: Creating Custom Test Statistics
text: Add test statistic statistics set:
code: # Single-event: add to SingleEventStatisticsSet single_stats <- SingleEventStatisticsSet$new() single_stats$add_test(WilcoxonARTest$new())  # Multi-event: add to MultiEventStatisticsSet multi_stats <- MultiEventStatisticsSet$new() multi_stats$add_test(KSTest$new())  # Or create a custom set from scratch custom_single <- StatisticsSetBase$new(   tests = list(ARTTest$new(), CARTTest$new(), WilcoxonARTest$new()) )

title: Creating Custom Test Statistics
text: package includes following built-test statistics: Single-event: - ARTTest – Abnormal Return t-test - CARTTest – Cumulative Abnormal Return t-test - BHARTTest – Buy--Hold Abnormal Return t-test Multi-event: - CSectTTest – Cross-Sectional t-test (AAR/CAAR) - PatellZTest – Patell standardized residual test - SignTest – Simple sign test - GeneralizedSignTest – Cowan (1992) generalized sign test - RankTest – Corrado (1989) rank test - BMPTest – Boehmer, Musumeci & Poulsen (1991) test - CalendarTimePortfolioTest – Calendar-time portfolio approach

Prepare and fit params <- ParameterSet$new(return_model = MarketModel$new()) task <- prepare_event_study(task, params)  # 4. Validate AFTER preparation (now windows are assigned) validate_task(task)  # 5. Fit models task <- fit_model(task, params)  # 6. Flag problematic events problems <- diag %>%   filter(shapiro_p < 0.05 | ljung_box_p < 0.05 | dw_stat < 1.5 | dw_stat > 2.5)  if (nrow(problems) > 0) {   cat("Events with diagnostic issues:\n")   print(problems %>% select(event_id, firm_symbol, shapiro_p, ljung_box_p, dw_stat)) } else {   cat("All events pass diagnostic checks.\n") }  # 8. Calculate statistics and test pre-trends task <- calculate_statistics(task, params) pretrend <- pretrend_test(task) print(pretrend)

title: Factor Models, GARCH, and Buy-and-Hold Abnormal Returns
text: simple Market Model regresses firm returns single market index. widely used, may miss systematic risk factors explain return variation. EventStudy package provides several alternatives: Factor models reduce estimation-window residual variance, yielding powerful tests. GARCH accounts volatility clustering. BHAR avoids bias summing daily abnormal returns long horizons.

Miller’s paper provides unified framework covering data structure, estimating equation, reference-period normalization, endpoint binning, heterogeneous treatment effects staggered adoption, pre-trend testing, inference. map concept EventStudy package’s panel module.

title: Panel Event Studies: A Guide Following Miller (2023)
text: Miller classifies panel event study settings along two dimensions: Single vs. staggered event dates — treated units receive treatment period, different cohorts adopt different times? Never-treated units present — set units remain untreated throughout sample? distinctions matter staggered adoption, combined heterogeneous treatment effects, can bias conventional two-way fixed effects (TWFE) estimators—point return Section 8.

title: Panel Event Studies: A Guide Following Miller (2023)
text: Thirty units observed 20 periods. Fifteen units treated period 10; fifteen never treated.
code: set.seed(42) n_units <- 30 n_periods <- 20 treat_period <- 10 true_effect <- 2.0  dataset_a <- tibble(   unit_id = rep(1:n_units, each = n_periods),   time_id = rep(1:n_periods, n_units) ) %>%   mutate(     # First 15 units are treated at period 10     treatment_time = ifelse(unit_id <= 15, treat_period, NA_integer_),     treated = ifelse(!is.na(treatment_time) & time_id >= treatment_time, 1, 0),     # Unit and time fixed effects + treatment effect + noise     unit_fe = rep(rnorm(n_units, 0, 1), each = n_periods),     time_fe = rep(rnorm(n_periods, 0, 0.5), n_units),     outcome = unit_fe + time_fe + true_effect * treated + rnorm(n() , 0, 1)   )

title: Panel Event Studies: A Guide Following Miller (2023)
text: Fifty units 20 periods. Three treatment cohorts adopt periods 8, 12, 16; fourth group never treated.
code: set.seed(123) n_units_b <- 50 n_periods_b <- 20  dataset_b <- tibble(   unit_id = rep(1:n_units_b, each = n_periods_b),   time_id = rep(1:n_periods_b, n_units_b) ) %>%   mutate(     # Assign cohorts: units 1-12 at t=8, 13-25 at t=12, 26-37 at t=16, rest never     treatment_time = case_when(       unit_id <= 12             ~ 8L,       unit_id > 12 & unit_id <= 25 ~ 12L,       unit_id > 25 & unit_id <= 37 ~ 16L,       TRUE                      ~ NA_integer_     ),     treated = ifelse(!is.na(treatment_time) & time_id >= treatment_time, 1, 0),     # Heterogeneous effects: early adopters have larger effects     true_te = case_when(       treatment_time == 8  ~ 3.0,       treatment_time == 12 ~ 2.0,       treatment_time == 16 ~ 1.0,       TRUE                 ~ 0     ),     unit_fe = rep(rnorm(n_units_b, 0, 1), each = n_periods_b),     time_fe = rep(rnorm(n_periods_b, 0, 0.5), n_units_b),     outcome = unit_fe + time_fe + true_te * treated + rnorm(n(), 0, 1)   )

title: Panel Event Studies: A Guide Following Miller (2023)
text: Miller presents general dynamic specification panel event studies: Yit=αi+γt+∑j≠j*δj⋅Ditj+εitY_{} = \alpha_i + \gamma_t + \sum_{j \neq j^*} \delta_j \cdot D_{}^j + \varepsilon_{} : αi\alpha_i unit fixed effects, absorbing time-invariant differences across units; γt\gamma_t time fixed effects, absorbing common shocks affect units given period; DitjD_{}^j event-time indicator equal 1 unit ii exactly jj periods treatment date time tt; j*j^* omitted reference period (normalized zero); δj\delta_j treatment effect event time jj, measured relative reference period. EventStudy package implements equation estimate_panel_event_study(). method argument selects variant, leads, lags, base_period control event-time window normalization.

what: Static TWFE: The Single-Coefficient Model (Miller Section II.A)
title: Panel Event Studies: A Guide Following Miller (2023)
text: simplest panel event study specification restricts post-treatment effects single coefficient β\beta: Yit=αi+γt+β⋅Dit+εitY_{} = \alpha_i + \gamma_t + \beta \cdot D_{} + \varepsilon_{} Dit=1D_{} = 1 unit ii treated time tt (post-treatment), 0 otherwise. coefficient β\beta average treatment effect treated (ATT) assumption treatment effect constant across post-treatment periods cohorts. static model good starting point, assumes homogeneous effects. treatment effect varies time (e.g., growing fading), assumption can misleading. dynamic specification relaxes .
code: task_a <- estimate_panel_event_study(task_a, method = "static_twfe") task_a$results$coefficients #>   term  estimate std.error statistic  p.value #>   ATT   2.01     0.15      13.4      <0.001

what: Dynamic TWFE: Event-Time Coefficients (Miller Section II.B)
title: Panel Event Studies: A Guide Following Miller (2023)
text: dynamic specification estimates separate coefficient δj\delta_j event-time period, allowing us trace treatment effect path: pre-treatment coefficients (j<0j < 0) close zero parallel trends assumption, post-treatment coefficients (j≥0j \geq 0) capture treatment effect dynamics. plot shows point estimates confidence intervals event time, vertical dashed line separating pre- post-treatment periods.
code: task_a <- estimate_panel_event_study(   task_a,   method      = "dynamic_twfe",   leads       = 5,   lags        = 5,   base_period = -1 )  task_a$results$coefficients #>   relative_time estimate std.error statistic p.value #>              -5    0.02     0.30      0.07    0.95 #>              -4   -0.10     0.28     -0.36    0.72 #>              ... #>              -1    0.00     0.00        NA      NA #>               0    1.95     0.22      8.86   <0.001 #>               1    2.03     0.23      8.83   <0.001 #>              ... plot_panel_event_study(task_a, title = "Dynamic TWFE - Single Cohort")

what: Reference Period and Normalization (Miller Section III)
title: Panel Event Studies: A Guide Following Miller (2023)
text: One event-time indicator must omitted avoid perfect collinearity unit time fixed effects. reference period j*j^*, coefficients δj\delta_j interpreted relative . Miller emphasizes choice reference period merely mechanical necessity—substantive implications. default base_period = -1 normalizes period immediately treatment, δ0\delta_0 captures immediate treatment effect. Alternative choices include: base_period = -2, coefficient j=−1j = -1 becomes interpretable test anticipation effects: units begin reacting treatment, coefficient non-zero. Miller also discusses extended reference periods multiple pre-treatment periods pooled reference group. package normalizes single period, can approximate checking pre-treatment coefficients jointly close zero (see Section 9 pre-trend testing).
code: # Normalize to two periods before treatment task_a <- estimate_panel_event_study(   task_a,   method      = "dynamic_twfe",   leads       = 5,   lags        = 5,   base_period = -2 )

text: formal approach joint F-test null hypothesis pre-treatment coefficients equal zero:
code: coefs <- task_a$results$coefficients pre_treatment <- coefs %>%   filter(relative_time < 0, relative_time != -1)  # exclude base period  if (nrow(pre_treatment) > 0) {   f_stat <- sum(pre_treatment$estimate^2 / pre_treatment$std.error^2) /     nrow(pre_treatment)   p_value <- pf(f_stat, df1 = nrow(pre_treatment),                 df2 = task_a$results$model$df.residual,                 lower.tail = FALSE)   cat("Joint pre-trend F-stat:", round(f_stat, 3), "\n")   cat("p-value:               ", round(p_value, 4), "\n") }

title: Panel Event Studies: A Guide Following Miller (2023)
text: Miller warns absence evidence evidence absence. non-significant pre-trend test prove parallel trends—may simply reflect low statistical power. Conversely, small statistically significant pre-treatment coefficients may substantively unimportant. Researchers : Report pre-treatment coefficients confidence intervals. Contextualize magnitude pre-trends relative estimated treatment effects. Consider sensitivity analyses (e.g., Rambachan & Roth, 2023) violations parallel trends affect conclusions.

title: Panel Event Studies: A Guide Following Miller (2023)
text: Miller recommends reporting just treatment effect estimates, also counterfactual outcomes—treated units’ outcomes absent treatment. helps readers assess magnitude plausibility estimates. dynamic model, counterfactual treated unit event time jj observed outcome minus estimated effect: gap observed counterfactual lines treatment date visualizes estimated treatment effect.
code: # Construct counterfactual for treated units coef_lookup <- task_a$results$coefficients %>%   select(relative_time, estimate) %>%   deframe()  counterfactual <- dataset_a %>%   filter(!is.na(treatment_time)) %>%   mutate(     rel_time = time_id - treatment_time,     delta_hat = coef_lookup[as.character(rel_time)],     delta_hat = ifelse(is.na(delta_hat), 0, delta_hat),     outcome_counterfactual = outcome - delta_hat   )  # Plot observed vs counterfactual counterfactual_summary <- counterfactual %>%   group_by(time_id) %>%   summarise(     observed       = mean(outcome),     counterfactual = mean(outcome_counterfactual),     .groups = "drop"   )  ggplot(counterfactual_summary, aes(x = time_id)) +   geom_line(aes(y = observed, color = "Observed"), linewidth = 0.8) +   geom_line(aes(y = counterfactual, color = "Counterfactual"),             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +   geom_vline(xintercept = 10, linetype = "dotted", color = "red") +   labs(     title = "Observed vs Counterfactual Outcomes (Treated Units)",     x     = "Time Period",     y     = "Mean Outcome",     color = NULL   ) +   theme_minimal()

title: Panel Event Studies: A Guide Following Miller (2023)
text: Drawing Miller (2023), checklist panel event study research: Classify setting. Single cohort staggered? Never-treated controls available? Start dynamic specification. Plot event-time coefficients collapsing static estimate. Inspect pre-trends. Report pre-treatment coefficients visually joint test. Choose reference period deliberately. base_period = -1 standard; consider whether anticipation effects warrant earlier reference. Report endpoint binning. transparent event times binned test sensitivity different window widths. Use appropriate estimators staggered designs. treatment timing varies effects may heterogeneous, use Sun & Abraham similar heterogeneity-robust estimators instead TWFE. Report counterfactual outcomes. Show happened absent treatment. Cluster standard errors appropriately. Cluster unit level ensure enough clusters (42–50+) reliable inference. Test robustness. Vary window width, reference period, estimator. Report results multiple specifications.

text: Synthetic control methods (Abadie Gardeazabal, 2003; Abadie, Diamond, Hainmueller, 2010) provide data-driven approach construct counterfactual single treated unit weighted combination donor (control) units. particularly useful : single treated unit (e.g., one firm, one country) traditional event study many events possible want visualize treatment effect gap actual synthetic trajectories EventStudy package implements synthetic control estimation two optimization methods includes placebo test inference.

title: Synthetic Control Methods
text: Synthetic control requires: - Treated unit: time series outcome treated unit - Donor pool: time series outcomes potential control units - Treatment time: intervention occurs

title: Time-Varying Beta Models: Rolling Window and DCC-GARCH
text: standard market model assumes constant beta estimation window. practice, betas can vary time due changing firm risk, leverage, market conditions. EventStudy package provides two time-varying beta models: RollingWindowModel: Rolling OLS estimation (additional dependencies) DCCGARCHModel: Dynamic Conditional Correlation GARCH (requires rmgarch)

title: Time-Varying Beta Models: Rolling Window and DCC-GARCH
text: RollingWindowModel estimates alpha beta using rolling OLS window estimation period. parameters last window used event-window prediction.

title: Time-Varying Beta Models: Rolling Window and DCC-GARCH
code: library(EventStudy)  task <- EventStudyTask$new(firm_data, index_data, request)  ps <- ParameterSet$new(   return_model = RollingWindowModel$new(window_size = 60) ) task <- run_event_study(task, ps)

title: Time-Varying Beta Models: Rolling Window and DCC-GARCH
text: window_size parameter controls width rolling window. smaller window captures faster parameter changes noisier:
code: # Shorter window: more responsive but noisier rw_short <- RollingWindowModel$new(window_size = 30, min_obs = 20)  # Longer window: smoother but slower to adapt rw_long <- RollingWindowModel$new(window_size = 120, min_obs = 60)

title: Time-Varying Beta Models: Rolling Window and DCC-GARCH
text: fitting, can inspect time series rolling parameters:
code: ps <- ParameterSet$new(   return_model = RollingWindowModel$new(window_size = 60) ) task <- run_event_study(task, ps)  # Access rolling parameters from the fitted model model_data <- task$data_tbl$data[[1]] model_obj <- task$data_tbl$model[[1]] stats <- model_obj$statistics  # Rolling betas over the estimation window plot(stats$rolling_betas, type = "l",      main = "Rolling Beta over Estimation Window",      xlab = "Window Index", ylab = "Beta") abline(h = stats$beta, lty = 2, col = "red")  # final beta

title: Time-Varying Beta Models: Rolling Window and DCC-GARCH
text: position estimation window, rolling OLS regression fit: Rfirm,t=αw+βwRmarket,t+εtR_{firm,t} = \alpha_w + \beta_w R_{market,t} + \varepsilon_t ww indexes windows size window_size. produces time series αt\alpha_t, βt\beta_t, σt\sigma_t. parameters last rolling window used predict expected returns event window. Abnormal returns computed : ARt=Rfirm,t−(α̂last+β̂lastRmarket,t)AR_t = R_{firm,t} - (\hat{\alpha}_{last} + \hat{\beta}_{last} R_{market,t})

title: Time-Varying Beta Models: Rolling Window and DCC-GARCH

title: Volume and Volatility Event Studies
text: Traditional event studies focus price-based abnormal returns. However, corporate events often affect trading volume return volatility even net price effect ambiguous. example, earnings announcement may trigger heavy trading volatility spikes without moving price much either direction. Volume volatility event studies capture information-content effects price-based methods can miss. EventStudy package provides two dedicated models: models plug standard pipeline (prepare_event_study() → fit_model() → calculate_statistics()) compatible existing test statistics.
code: library(EventStudy) library(dplyr) library(ggplot2)

title: Volume and Volatility Event Studies

code: set.seed(42)  n <- 300 firm_tbl <- tibble(   symbol      = "FIRM_A",   date        = format(seq(as.Date("2014-06-01"), by = "day",                            length.out = n), "%d.%m.%Y"),   adjusted    = 100 * cumprod(1 + rnorm(n, 0.0003, 0.015)),   firm_volume = pmax(0, rnorm(n, mean = 1e6, sd = 2e5)) )  index_tbl <- tibble(   symbol   = "INDEX_1",   date     = firm_tbl$date,   adjusted = 1000 * cumprod(1 + rnorm(n, 0.0002, 0.012)) )  request_tbl <- tibble(   event_id = 1L, firm_symbol = "FIRM_A", index_symbol = "INDEX_1",   event_date = firm_tbl$date[200], group = "Earnings",   event_window_start = -10L, event_window_end = 10L,   shift_estimation_window = -11L, estimation_window_length = 150L )  # --- Price study --- task_price <- EventStudyTask$new(firm_tbl, index_tbl, request_tbl) params_price <- ParameterSet$new(return_model = MarketModel$new()) task_price <- run_event_study(task_price, params_price)  # --- Volume study --- task_vol <- EventStudyTask$new(firm_tbl, index_tbl, request_tbl) params_vol <- ParameterSet$new(return_model = VolumeModel$new()) params_vol$study_type <- "volume" task_vol <- task_vol |>   prepare_event_study(params_vol) |>   fit_model(params_vol) |>   calculate_statistics(params_vol)  # --- Volatility study --- task_volat <- EventStudyTask$new(firm_tbl, index_tbl, request_tbl) params_volat <- ParameterSet$new(return_model = VolatilityModel$new()) params_volat$study_type <- "volatility" task_volat <- task_volat |>   prepare_event_study(params_volat) |>   fit_model(params_volat) |>   calculate_statistics(params_volat) # Extract tidy ARs from each study ar_price  <- tidy.EventStudyTask(task_price, type = "ar") %>%   mutate(study = "Price (AR)") ar_vol    <- tidy.EventStudyTask(task_vol, type = "ar") %>%   mutate(study = "Volume (Abnormal Log-Volume)") ar_volat  <- tidy.EventStudyTask(task_volat, type = "ar") %>%   mutate(study = "Volatility (Variance Ratio - 1)")  combined <- bind_rows(ar_price, ar_vol, ar_volat)  ggplot(combined, aes(x = relative_index, y = abnormal_returns)) +   geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +   geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted", colour = "red", alpha = 0.6) +   geom_col(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +   facet_wrap(~ study, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +   labs(     title = "Price, Volume, and Volatility Event Study",     x     = "Relative Time to Event",     y     = "Abnormal Measure"   ) +   theme_minimal()

what: Degenerate-Input Contract for EventStudy Models — degenerate-input-contract
title: Degenerate-Input Contract for EventStudy Models — degenerate-input-contract
text: degenerate-input contract defines EventStudy return models behave estimation data degenerate. Two modes supported: Lenient (default): model sets is_fitted = FALSE, emits exactly one warning() per (event_id, firm_symbol) per fit call, propagates NA abnormal returns downstream statistics. event silently dropped; zeros never substituted NA. Strict: model raises descriptive stop() error naming component, event_id, firm_symbol, plus specific reason degeneracy. Configuration: Via ParameterSet: ParameterSet$new(degenerate_handling = "strict") Via package option: options(EventStudy.degenerate_handling = "strict") ParameterSet field takes precedence package option; neither set, default "lenient" mode used. Degenerate conditions covered: Fewer 2 finite observations estimation window     (insufficient observations OLS). Zero near-zero variance index returns     (sd < .Machine$double.eps), making OLS estimation undefined. Single-event group (relevant multi-event statistics;     applied Phase 2). NA propagation upstream pipeline steps. NA propagation semantics: is_fitted = FALSE, model$abnormal_returns() returns tibble abnormal_returns = NA_real_ rows. downstream test statistics depend fitted models receive NA inputs propagate NA outputs. event retained output tibble — never silently dropped.
